segments.text: All right. So, good morning. Welcome. I'm Jenny-May Coffey.
So, I'm here from the Social Services and Community Select Committee this morning,
and I welcome you to give us your
intro to the Legislation Definitions of Woman Amendment Bill.
If you want to leave any time for questions towards the end, please feel free to do
so. I do understand you are on a tight schedule.
Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Really appreciate being here.
And firstly, I would like to acknowledge the work of the committee and thank every
New Zealander who's taken time to make a submission and contribute to
exactly the process that Parliament exists to provide.
Democracy doesn't stop after first reading.
It continues here in committee rooms like this one, where ideas are tested,
challenged, and hopefully improved.
When I introduced this bill, I said it was about legal certainty.
I believe that even more strongly today.
Some have tried to portray this bill as though it's about denying people dignity.
It is not. Some have claimed it's about removing rights. It is not.
And some have suggested that because these words have existed for centuries,
Parliament has no need to define them.
But if that were true, we would not have received tens of thousands of submissions
arguing passionately over what these words mean.
The very existence of this debate demonstrates why legislative clarity is needed.
This bill addresses a straightforward question.
When Parliament uses the words "woman," "man," "female," and "male" in New Zealand
law, what do those words mean? That is not a philosophical question.
It is a legal one.
The law depends on clear language, rights, obligations, exemptions, sporting
categories, prisons, healthcare, data collection, privacy protections, and women's
services all rely upon these terms having stable meanings.
If a fundamental legal language becomes uncertain, then uncertainty spreads, and
that uncertainty is not merely theoretical.
It is women who feel the consequences first.
Women's sport depends on knowing who the female category is for.
Women's refuges, hospital wards, changing rooms, prisons, and sex-based
healthcare all rely upon the law being able to recognize what a woman is.
For more than a century, New Zealand women have fought to secure protections that
recognize our biological reality.
Those hard-won rights should not become uncertain simply because Parliament has
allowed the meaning of the word "woman" to become contested.
Parliament, not government agencies, not advisory bodies, and not the courts, has
the responsibility to define the words our laws rely upon.
That has always been the purpose of this bill.
This bill does not create sex-based rights.
Those rights already exist throughout our law.
What it does is strengthen the legal foundations that support them.
If the foundation becomes unstable, eventually everything built upon it becomes
unstable, too.
Now, I also want to acknowledge something important.
One of the strengths of the Select Committee process is that it allows legislation
to mature. A member's bill begins a conversation. It is rarely the final word.
Many submissions accepted the objective of the bill while arguing that it could be
drafted more effectively. I welcome that approach.
Supporting a bill does not mean pretending it cannot be improved.
In fact, if we're going to legislate in an area as important as this, we have an
obligation to get it right.
One of the most persuasive recommendations I've received is that the legislation
should define sex first before defining woman, man, female, and male, and I think
that's a sensible refinement.
If the law relies upon biological sex, then it should clearly explain what it means
by that concept. Otherwise, uncertainty simply shifts from one word to
another. So instead of arguing over woman, people begin arguing over biological.
Likewise, I think there is merit in making it absolutely clear that age,
infertility, injury, disease, developmental conditions, or medical treatment
do not alter a person's legal sex. Those circumstances do not create new
sexes, nor should they undermine the coherence of the legal categories Parliament
is establishing. Another helpful refinement concerns the phrase, "regardless of
gender identity."
The intention of including those words in the original bill was to make clear that
legal sex is not changed simply because someone identifies differently.
However, the feedback has persuaded me that the drafting can be more precise.
Rather than relying upon a contested phrase, it is better to state directly that
self-identification, medical treatment, or changes to administrative records do not
alter a person's legal sex for the purposes of legislation.
That says exactly what Parliament intends without creating unnecessary ambiguity.
If definitions can simply be displaced whenever someone argues that the surrounding
context requires a different meaning, then we risk recreating precisely
the uncertainty that prompted this legislation in the first place.
Some submitters have argued that this bill will somehow remove protections from
transgender New Zealanders. I do not accept that characterization.
Defining sex for legal purposes is not the same thing as removing protections
against discrimination. Those are separate legal questions.
People should be protected from unfair discrimination.
They should be treated with dignity and respect.
Nothing in this bill prevents Parliament from ensuring those protections continue.
In fact, several submissions suggested that greater clarity between biological sex
and gender identity could improve certainty for everyone, and I think that is a
constructive contribution to this discussion.
But rights are not protected by pretending competing rights never arise.
Parliament balances rights every day.
Protecting transgender New Zealanders from unfair discrimination does not require
us to erase or weaken sex-based rights that generations of women fought to
establish. We are capable of protecting both.
That is precisely what good law should do.
There's also been discussion about intersex people and differences of sexual
development. Again, these circumstances do not undermine the purpose of the
bill. Every area of law recognizes that different cases exist at
the margins. The existence of exceptional cases does not prevent Parliament from
defining general legal categories where those categories are necessary for the
administration of the law. We should acknowledge complexity where it
exists without abandoning clarity where clarity is required.
I introduced this bill because I believe women deserve laws that recognize
biological reality. We should never apologize for saying that women exist as a
biological class. The women who won the vote in 1893 knew what they were
fighting for. The women who secured equal pay, maternity protections, sex
discrimination laws, women's sport, women's refuges, and countless other
advantages and advances all understood that those protections existed because
women are a distinct biological reality Their achievements were not
won on behalf of an identity. They were won on behalf of women.
This bill stands in that same tradition.
It seeks to ensure that future generations inherit laws that remain capable of
recognizing the very people those protections were created to serve.
I believe men also deserve the same,
and I believe Parliament has both the authority and the responsibility to define
the legal language upon which so many rights and obligations depend.
This committee will do exactly what select committees are supposed to do.
It'll hear from New Zealanders. It'll test the arguments.
It will identify ways to make a good bill better, and I welcome the
improvements the committee will make because they reinforce, not weaken, the
purpose of the legislation.
The objective remains exactly as it was on the day I stood in the House at first
reading: to restore clarity, consistency, and certainty to New
Zealand law.
Words matter. Definitions matter. Women's rights matter.
Laws cannot protect what they cannot define.
If Parliament is unwilling to say what a woman is, then Parliament should not be
surprised when the legal protections built around women begin to weaken.
New Zealand has always been proud of its history as a pioneer for women.
We were the first self-governing nation to give women the vote.
We should also be proud to ensure that our laws continue to recognize women as a
biological reality. That is what this bill seeks to achieve.
Through reflecting public feedback, the committee has the opportunity to make it a
stronger bill, a clearer bill, and a more enduring bill. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
Thank you, committee.
All right. Thank you much, Jenny. Is there a question from Georgina?
Thank you. My question's around the word biological and what
the test is or what the means is for biological.
Is it to do with what chromosomes a person has?
Is it to do with what hormones the person has in their body, or is it to do with
what body parts the person has?
Well, I think if you are wanting a scientific answer, then perhaps I could point
you to a very good article in "Newsroom" just last week, which spoke to
a couple of scientists that went through that whole argument that you're
proposing. I think that's the best place, but I think if you want to
define women biologically, as this bill is seeking to do for the
necessary
results in terms of maintaining women's sex-based protections,
our unique privacy needs and requirements as women, then that's what
this bill is requiring to do. But in terms of specific scientific analysis, you're
best placed speaking to a scientist.
All right. So just to sup on that, just thinking of a scenario where someone is
assigned female at birth, but they have been living as a man for the past 30 years.
So they have been taking testosterone. They may have had surgery.
They present masculine. They would be excluded from women's sports because of their
testosterone levels, and they are listed as being male on their birth
certificate. That person, because they were assigned female at birth, would they be
using the women's bathroom?
Well, I think that identifying as a--
Sorry, can you just repeat that part of the question, kind of the-
Yeah. So someone who's been assigned-- Was born and assigned female when they were
born, but they've been living as a man for the past 30 years.
They've been taking testosterone, so they have facial hair.
They are muscular and have male characteristics, and they may have male written on
their birth certificate as allowed by our current legislation.
Is that person, under your legislation, classified as a
woman?
If you're biologically female, then you are a female.
So that person who cannot-
Sorry. I have a question from Caroline.
Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you
to the member.
So this bill you've talked about has come from women's interest groups, and you're
wanting to clarify legislation.
One of the motivations that was put in the
initial press release was around safety.
So there's a quote in here from the original press release that says, "This bill
would ensure our country moves away from the woke ideology that has crept in over
the last few years, undermining the protection, progression, and safety of women."
And I know that this is quite similar to the
framing that's come out of the UK, and this came very quickly after the ruling
happened over there. So if you could just tell me about your concerns for safety
for women.
Well, I think that safety is a concern for women.
We have an innate need to protect ourselves, and when you
have biological males coming into female-only spaces, that
presents
basically a boundary breach.
I know that New Zealand First has been-
Oh, sorry
... concerned about the bathroom legislation, but do you know if it's only
concerned-
Sorry, Caroline, we are at time.
Sorry. Thank you.
Sorry, Caroline. We are at time. But look, thank you, Jenny, for-
Thank you
... coming and making a submission to the committee this morning.
We look forward to hearing more on this bill.
Great. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair.
Thank you.
Thank you, committee.
